newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals -- High prices halt Japan copper trade.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals -- High prices halt Japan copper trade.

text.p: Trade in the Japanese physical copper market has ground to a halt due to strong cash prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME), triggered by a technical squeeze, traders said on Wednesday.

"There's hardly any business in the spot market," said a trader at one of Japan's major trading houses. "Because of a wide backwardation, the cash price is very high. The yen is also weak, and we are entering the summer holiday season."

In London overnight, the cash-to-threes backwardation ended at $250/$255 on Tuesday after flaring by $100 during Third Wednesday pricing on Monday. Tomorrow/next trading surged to a $24 backwardation -- just $1 short of the LME limit.
Traders said few were willing to buy copper especially as many expect prices to turn downwards next month when the backwardation is seen narrowing.
Another trader said: "The market doesn't look good. Nobody feels they have to buy when prices are so expensive. Under current circumstances people prefer to sell even at low premiums."
Traders said Japanese production of copper pipes was falling because of large air conditioner stocks in Japan and China, a major buyer of Japanese copper pipes.
Copper cable business was also hit by weak demand from the construction sector following a rise in Japan's national consumption tax in April, traders said.

A third trader added: "There are hardly any buyers in the Asian spot market, we can't expect domestic demand to recover in the short term. South Korea and Thailand are faring badly, Taiwan is stagnating and China has stopped spot buying as well."
However, the situation in Japan's physical aluminium and zinc market is a completely different matter, traders said.
Traders said premiums for spot aluminium remained high at $90-100 per tonne, with some starting to predict that premiums might stay at these high levels for a while.
"We're not getting enough metal (from abroad)," said one trader, adding Russian supplies were growing scarce.
The trader said aluminium stocks at Yokohama had dropped further to below 130,000 tonnes at the end of June -- well below usual levels of above 200,000 tonnes.

Traders said the zinc market was also tight as the increase in the sales tax has so far failed to dent strong demand for galvanized steel, particularly from the car, construction and home electronics industry.
"We heard some traders bought quite a lot of zinc from China over the last one to two weeks. We don't have enough metal," said one zinc trader at a trading house.
Yet traders said premiums for Chinese special high grade (SHG) zinc remained low at $20-30 per tonne as China was keen to boost exports while the prices were strong on the LME.
But some traders said China now faced difficulties in acquiring enough ore to raise its production, especially as their own mines were eagar to sell their output abroad to earn foreign currencies.

North Korea, on the other hand, seems to have little to offer as the country is being hit by a shortage in ore, electricity and foreign currency needed to revamp its production facilities, traders said.
"We heard from Chinese traders, who used to sell quite a lot of ore to North Korea, that they did not want to do business with them as it was uncertain if North Korea would pay up," said a trader.
